TransportPipes · the complete game design · version 1.4

TransportPipes 1.4

You start with an empty plot next to a Yard. You build mines, factories and pipes, sell to the market and trade with your Yard's neighbours at prices you set. Your research makes you very good at a few things, so friends who split the work grow faster. Together the town builds a Wonder, and the Wonder takes the whole town into the next Era, with new resources, new buildings and more room.

Your own placePick a free plot on the map, next to friends or anywhere. Start with an HQ, a trading post and 2,000 gold.
The YardFour plots share one Yard of 32×16 tiles. The people who live there are a crew, and they own the Yard together.
Only peopleThe market is the only player that isn't a person. It always buys and sells, but friends beat its prices.
Deep researchA research track takes about ten days and makes its chain fifteen times better. Basic tiers take minutes, the big ones days.
Towns and ErasSixteen players make a town. Each town reaches its next Era by finishing its own Wonder.
A ceiling you can seeBuildings stop at level 25. Every Era makes about four times the one before.

1 · The game in one minute

  1. You pick a plot. The start screen is the map. You click a free plot of 32×32 tiles in a town that is still in Era 1, next to a friend or wherever you like.
  2. You build from nothing. Wind Moilies and solar panels make energy, mines dig ore, factories turn it into ingots, bricks and glass. Pipes connect them, and goods flow every minute, also while you're away.
  3. You sell. Your trading post sells to the town's market. The market pays the full price for an amount of each good (your Hub Order) and less for floods. It also sells everything, at 2.5 times the price.
  4. You trade with your Yard. Your plot touches a Yard shared with three neighbours. A pipe to your Yard gate is all it takes: what a neighbour lacks is filled from your spare at the price you set, and the other way round. Every price between friends beats the market for both sides.
  5. Nobody has everything. Each plot lacks two of the eight land resources, a different two for each plot in a Yard. Any three neighbours together have everything.
  6. You get very good at a few things. Research tracks take days. A player who masters the Iron track makes fifteen times the iron of someone who didn't, with the same buildings, and the market buys more from a master. Friends who master different tracks sell each other what each lacks, and the four of them pay for one Monument that makes all four more productive.
  7. Your town moves on together. Sixteen players share a town and its market. The town builds its Era Wonder from the goods its players give. When it's finished, the whole town enters the next Era: a new raw resource, new goods, new buildings, a better pipe and more room. After five Eras the town launches its Space Elevator.

2 · Seven rules the game follows

Every part of this design was checked against these. When two ideas fight, the rule higher in the list wins.

RuleWhat it meansWhere you see it
1 · Fun alone, better with friends A solo player can reach every Era and finish every track. Friends who split the work get there sooner and earn more. Nobody is ever stuck because a friend stopped playing. The market always buys and sells; research by time; the Yard's Monument shared by its residents
2 · One balance at every size No number in the game depends on how many people play: not on the server, not in the town, not in the Yard. The game never makes up for having fewer people. More people get further because more people make more, never because a rule changes. Fixed Hub Orders, fixed Wonder and Monument sizes, no "quiet server" bonus, no "half the town" rule
3 · Only people No computer-run companies. The market is the one thing that isn't a person, and it never pretends to be one. Free plots are empty land; no Houses, stand-ins or caretakers
4 · Your own place You choose where you live, start from nothing, and nobody can touch what you built. Pick a spot on the map; moving is free; no destructive actions
5 · Everything flows Goods visibly move through pipes. You can tell what a plot does by looking at it. Pipes, the Yard's stalls, goods crossing the Yard
6 · Choices that matter What you research, which land you buy, who in the Yard makes what and how much you give the Wonder all change how your game goes. Research takes days; level cap; land lacks two resources
7 · Progress while away Everything keeps running offline. Coming back is a reward. Nothing is lost by not playing. Offline report, research and Wonders that wait for you

3 · Words

Plot
Your land: 32×32 tiles, in 16 parcels of 8×8. You start with four parcels (16×16) against the Yard.
Parcel
8×8 tiles of land. You buy them one at a time, each 2.5 times the price of the one before, one more every second Company Level.
Yard
The 32×16 space between four plots. Its residents trade there, build Monuments there and own it together.
Crew
The people who live around one Yard (one to four). Joining a Yard means joining its crew.
Yard gate
Where your plot meets the Yard. A pipe from your buildings to your gate is your connection to the Yard.
Town
Four Yards (16 plots) around a hub. A town has one market, one Era and one Era Wonder. The first town is the Capital, and every town has a name (Ironvale, Copperbrook…).
Hub
The town's centre: the market, the Wonder site, statues and the town board.
Market
The town's buyer and seller of everything. It pays a good's base price, up to your Hub Order, and sells at 2.5× the base.
Hub Order
How much of a good the market buys from you per minute at the full price. Beyond it, the price falls.
Outskirts
The land between a town's Yards. From Era 2, each plot can buy nine outskirts parcels set aside for it.
Era
A stage of a town: Steam & Iron, Electric, Oil & Machines, Electronics, Space Age. Your own Era is the highest Era you have reached.
Era Wonder
The town's big building project. Finishing it moves the town into the next Era.
Monument
A Yard's own building project, one site per Era, built with gold in stages without end; every stage gives every resident a perk.
Track
A research line for one chain (Iron, Power, Glass…), nine tiers over about ten days.
Base price
A good's reference price. Every price in the game is a multiple of it.

4 · The world: plot, Yard, town

A Yard group

  • The Yard is 32×16 tiles, wider than high, five times the size of today's Yard.
  • One plot sits above it and one below, sharing the Yard's long sides. Two more sit at its ends.
  • Every plot's start area (its four first parcels, 16×16) lies against the Yard, with the Yard gate in the middle of that edge. Your first pipe reaches the Yard.
  • The plots above and below get 32 tiles of Yard edge, the ones at the ends 16. That changes only how much Yard edge each has, not what they can trade.

A town

  • Four Yard groups, so 16 plots, around the hub (68×52 tiles): the market, the Era Wonder's building site, statues and past Wonders.
  • Two roads cross the town. Links between Yards run along them.
  • The gaps between the groups are the outskirts: twelve patches of 32×24 tiles, 144 parcels. Each plot has nine of them set aside for it (§5).
  • Around each town lies wilderness, 128 tiles to the next town, with rivers, mountains and rich deposits. Where the roads leave the town stand four town gates, where lines from other towns arrive (§20).

The world

  • Towns spiral out from the Capital, the first town. The Capital is a town like the others; it's just the oldest.
  • A new town opens when every Era-1 town has fewer than two free plots. Newcomers always start in an Era-1 town, so there is always one with room.
  • The world map shows every town with its name, its Era, its Wonder's progress and how many plots are free.
  • Towns lie 128 tiles apart, four times today's distance, so there's room between them for long lines, outposts and what comes later. How the wilderness and the towns' dealings with each other work is the one part left open (§20).

5 · Your land

What every plot has, and what it lacks

There are eight land resources besides the ones every plot has. Each plot has six of them, and lacks one Era-1 basic and one later resource:

Every plot hasEach plot lacks one of…and one of
water, iron ore, wood (forest), wind, sun copper ore · coal · stone · sand bauxite (Era 2) · oil (Era 3) · rare earth (Era 4) · titanium ore (Era 5)
  • In a Yard the four plots lack different ones, so any three neighbours together have everything. Who lacks what is dealt per Yard when the world is made, and the plot's card shows it before you pick it.
  • The first hour is the same for everyone: every plot has wind, sun, water and iron ore.
  • A missing resource is a nudge, not a wall. You buy it from a neighbour at their price, from the market at 2.5×, from your outskirts (they hold every resource) or, much later, you seed it with a Terraformer.
  • The resources of later Eras are on the land from the start, as sleeping deposits with a small Era badge. You can see what you'll mine in Era 3 when you pick the plot.
  • Each plot has one rich deposit (★4) of something it has: its strength, also on its card. Other deposits are ★1 to ★3. Richness multiplies what a mine digs.

Terrain

Grass—everything

Red hillsbauxite (Era 2)no 3×3 buildings

Parcels

  • 16 parcels of 8×8. You start with the four against the Yard, with your HQ and trading post next to the gate.
  • You buy the other twelve in any order, as long as the new parcel touches land you own. Choosing which one is a real decision: the beach for sand, or the hill for wind?
  • The first costs 20,000 gold and each one 2.5 times the last (the twelfth: 477 million). Company Level limits how many you may own: the 5th parcel at Level 5, then one more every second level, the 16th at Level 27. A regular player has the whole plot around day 21 (§17).
  • Pipes may cross parcels you haven't bought, so the Yard gate is always in reach. Buildings need bought land.

The outskirts (from Era 2)

  • Each plot has nine outskirts parcels set aside for it, next to its own land, as the picture shows. Only you can buy yours, so a player in the middle of a town has the same room as one at the edge.
  • They open when your town reaches Era 2 and you've researched Survey the outskirts. The first costs 100 million gold, each one 1.4 times the last (the ninth: 1.5 billion): the big land purchase of Era 2. A regular player has all nine about nine days into Era 2 (§17).
  • The outskirts hold every land resource at ★2–★3, so a solo player can make up for what their plot lacks.
  • They count as your plot: same pipes, same buildings. When you move, they're bought back for half their price (§18).

Later Eras add more room in other directions: the Deep Level under your plot in Era 3, and outposts in the wilderness in Era 4.

6 · Starting: pick your spot

1Open the gameOr a friend's link. It opens the map at their plot.
2The mapThe real world map, zoomed out. Free plots glow in Era-1 towns. Taken plots show their company, level and Yard banner.
3A plot's cardWhat the land has and lacks, its strength, the Yard (who lives there, open or closed, its Monuments) and the town (its Era and Wonder).
4Name and colourYour company's name and colour. In a closed Yard, this sends a request instead.
5PlayAs a guest if you like. You can keep the company with a name and password later.
  • Newcomers start in an Era-1 town. Towns in a later Era are shown greyed out with their Era, and say why.
  • Pick for me chooses a free plot in an open Yard whose residents played in the last three days.
  • Find a player searches by name and flies the map to them.
  • Your link ("Play next to me") opens the map at your Yard, and lets the first player who uses it settle in your Yard even when it's closed. It works for seven days. Nothing is held: if your Yard fills up before your friend comes, the map shows the nearest free plots instead.
  • If a friend's town is in a later Era, their link says so and offers the nearest Era-1 town. You can still trade with that friend over the Exchange from day one.

The first hour

You start with your HQ, your trading post next to the Yard gate, and 2,000 gold. Nothing else is built. Loady, the game's smiley mascot, guides the first hour one step at a time, and the Next steps card always shows the three best things to do.

WhenWhat happensYou learn

7 · The Yard and your crew

The crew

  • The people who live around a Yard are its crew, one to four of them. Moving in makes you a member; moving away ends it. There are no codes, invites to manage or member limits beyond the four plots.
  • The first resident names the Yard (the crew's name), picks its banner colour and chooses open (anyone may settle on a free plot) or closed (a newcomer asks, and a resident says yes). Open is the default.
  • Every resident is an owner. Once more people live there, each of them can open or close the Yard, accept requests, start a Monument and place decorations. Nobody can be thrown out: an unhappy player moves away.
  • A request waits three days. The player who asked can play elsewhere in the meantime and moves in for free when a resident says yes.
  • A closed Yard stays closed, also when everyone in it stopped playing. Pick for me never sends a newcomer there.
  • The crew has its own chat, its banner on its plots, and the Plan board on the Yard's fence: each resident pins "I make…" and "I need…" with one tap per good.

What makes the Yard special

Trading in the Yard

  • A pipe to your Yard gate connects you. The Yard fills what a neighbour's buildings lack from your spare, and the other way round, every minute, offline too.
  • Inside the Yard you pay your neighbour's crew price, which every seller sets (§8). No fees, and no losses beyond your own pipe.
  • Fair when short: buyers keep the share they had over the last seven days, so nobody's factory stops overnight because a neighbour built more. New demand shares the rest.
  • Your stall shows what you sell, your crew price and a "wanted" sign for what you'd buy.

Building in the Yard

  • Workshops (from Level 10): each resident may put their own buildings on up to 64 tiles of the Yard's ends. A building in the Yard is connected to every resident without pipes, so a Steel Mill there takes one neighbour's ingots and another's coal directly. Workshops belong to whoever built them and move with them.
  • The Depot (from Level 10): the crew's shared storage. You put goods in for the crew; a neighbour takes them at your crew price. It is also where the crew piles goods for the Wonder.
  • Monuments, one site per Era, built with gold by any resident in stages without end (§13), and decorations placed by anyone.
When the last resident leavesThe Yard's own buildings (Monuments, the Depot, decorations) are torn down: they belonged to the crew, and the crew is gone. The last player to leave is warned before they confirm. Workshops always go with their owner.

A Yard of one

A solo player in an empty Yard has all of it: their stall, their 64 tiles of workshops, the Depot and the Monument. Nothing is resized for one (rule 2): the Monument costs a solo player what it costs a crew of four, so four friends who share it pay a quarter each. Pick for me prefers Yards where people play, so a newcomer who wants company finds it.

8 · Trading

Goods change hands in four ways. All four run every minute, offline too, and all of them pay in gold for goods that were really made:

The market

Your trading post sells everything to the town's market and can buy from it. It pays the base price up to your Hub Order and less beyond it; it sells at 2.5×.

Your Yard

What a neighbour's buildings lack is filled from your spare, and the other way round, at the price each seller sets for the crew. No contracts, no clicks.

Links

Standing deals with named players in other Yards of your town: a good, an amount an hour, a price.

The Exchange

List goods from your storages for every town, or buy what others list. Goods travel by cargo, and 4% leaves the game.

Gifts to your Yard's Monument and your town's Wonder are a fifth way goods leave your plot. They pay no gold (§13).

The market

Each town has a market in its hub. It buys every good of the town's Era and older, and sells the same goods.

  • Your Hub Order is how much of a good the market buys from you at the full base price each minute. It is yours alone: nobody else's sales change your price, and nobody shares it.
  • Every Era-1 good has a Hub Order worth 1,000 gold a minute at its base price, and every good of a later Era four times as much as one Era before. When your town reaches a later Era, the older goods' Hub Orders grow by half for each Era since.
  • Your trading post's level raises every Hub Order by 10% a level, to 9.85 times at level 25. Upgrading the post is how you grow your market. The post has no other limit: it sells everything that reaches it.
  • Beyond your Hub Order the price falls. Selling twice the Hub Order pays 1.41 times as much, four times pays twice as much, sixteen times four times as much. From sixteen times on, every further unit pays a quarter of the base price.
  • The market sells every good of the town's Era and older at 2.5 times the base price, without limit, to any building whose owner allows imports of that good.
  • These numbers are the same in every town, on every server, whatever the number of players (rule 2).

Worked example: Ben's iron ingots

Ben's trading post is at level 10, so his Hub Orders are 2.36 times the base: 168 iron ingots a minute (1,000 g ÷ 14 g × 2.36). His factories make 500 a minute, three times that. The market pays him 14 × √(168 × 500) = 4,060 gold a minute, an average of 8.1 g an ingot instead of 14. Each extra ingot now adds only 4.1 g. So Ben sells more of his ingots to his crew (who use them for levels, §9), upgrades his trading post, or puts the spare in the Wonder. The game shows each of these on the ingots' row.

Your prices

  • For every good you sell to players you set a price between the market's two prices, 1× to 2.5× the base, so trading with a friend is never worse than the market for either side.
  • A public price for everyone (default 1.3×), a crew price for your Yard (default 1.15×), and special prices for named players ("Ben: 1.0×"). A buyer always pays the lowest of the prices that apply to them.
  • Price rises wait an hour, and the buyers are told. Cuts count at once.
  • There are no free gifts between players, and gold never moves except as the price of goods that were really made. The lowest price (1.0×) is what the market would pay you anyway. That, the price band and the one-hour rule are the guards against a second account feeding the first.

The Yard, minute by minute

Trading in the Yard needs one thing: a pipe from your buildings to your Yard gate. From then on, the game does this every minute, for every good:

  1. Your own first. Your own buildings use what your own buildings make. What they can't use is your spare; what they need and don't get is your want. A want also counts what your storages keep for your next level or building.
  2. Links next. Standing deals with other Yards are filled before the Yard.
  3. Then the Yard. Each resident's want is filled from the others' spare, the seller with the lowest price for that buyer first. With equal prices, the seller who supplied that buyer before goes first, so supplies are steady.
  4. Fair when short. If the spare doesn't cover all wants, each buyer first gets the share it had over the last seven days, and new demand shares what's left. Nobody's factory stops overnight because a neighbour built more.
  5. Through the pipes. The goods run from the seller's buildings to the seller's gate, across the Yard, and from the buyer's gate to the buyer's buildings. Each side loses its own pipe's loss. The buyer pays for what arrives at their gate, at the seller's price, each minute.
  6. What's still wanted comes from the buyer's storages, then from the market at 2.5× if the buyer allows imports of that good; otherwise the building slows down and says why.
  7. What's still spare goes to the seller's storages' keeps, to the Wonder or Monument if "give" is on for that good, then to the market through the trading post, then to storage. When everything is full, the building slows down. Nothing is ever destroyed.
Worked example: one minute in a Yard on day 9

Ana (lacks copper ore), Ben (lacks coal), Cleo (lacks stone) and Dev (lacks sand) share a Yard. All crew prices are the default 1.15×.

Links: trading across the town

  • From Level 12, a link joins you to one named player in another Yard of your town: a pipe along the roads, laid automatically, paid per tile by its tier, losing a little per tile as every pipe does.
  • A link is a standing deal: a good, an amount per hour and a price (the seller's special or public price). It comes before the Yard in the order above, so it is reliable.
  • Up to 12 links. A link has a two-hour tank at the buyer's end, so a short gap never stops a factory.
  • From Era 3, trunk lines carry a Yard's links to other towns (§11).

The Exchange: trading with every town

  • From Level 12 you can list goods from your storages on the Exchange, at a price within the band, or buy what others list, in any town. It is how towns trade with each other from the start.
  • Goods travel by cargo: about an hour to the next town, longer further away (a Cargo Depot halves it, trains in Era 3 again). A 4% fee is taken out of the game.
  • You can only buy goods of your own Era or older.

Where your goods go

A building's spare, in this order

  1. Your own buildings on the same pipes
  2. Your links
  3. The Yard: neighbours who want it
  4. What your storages keep (today's orders, your next level or building, a pile you set)
  5. The Wonder or a Monument, for goods you switched to "give"
  6. Your trading post: the market
  7. Your storages, until full
  8. Nowhere left: the building slows down. Nothing is wasted.

A building's need, in this order

  1. Your own buildings on the same pipes
  2. Your links
  3. The Yard: the cheapest neighbour first
  4. Your storages
  5. The market at 2.5×, if you allow imports

What trading is worth

In the model (§17), paid trade between four friends in a Yard is 1% to 14% of their income: a neighbour's coal or sand in the first days, goods for levels from the second week, Era 2's chains after. The gold that changes hands is small next to what the market pays. What it buys is not: a Smelter that loses 27 g a minute on market copper ore earns 20 g on a friend's, and the glass for a level costs a plot without sand less than half as much from a neighbour (1.15×) as from the market (2.5×). Together with the Yard's Monument it puts a crew 21% ahead of the same players alone by day 14 and 12% by day 28.

9 · Buildings, levels and pipes

  • Placement: on your bought land, on fitting terrain (a mine needs its deposit, a pump a shore). Footprints are 1×1, 2×2 or 3×3. A building costs gold, and from Era 2 also goods; it takes seconds in Era 1 and hours in Era 5, with scaffolding and a crane.
  • Only pipes connect. Buildings that touch a pipe trade over it. Goods never pass through a building.
  • Moving your own buildings is free (a short rebuild). Demolishing returns half the gold, all of it with a Recycler.
  • Copies: every copy of the same building costs 7% more than the last (the 20th Wind Moily 723 g, the 40th 2,800 g), so you grow both by building more and by levelling up, and a plot of many kinds beats a plot of one.
  • Evolve in place: a building with a successor (Wind Moily → Big Turbine, Coal Plant → Steam Turbine, Solar Panel → Solar Farm, Small Factory → Big Factory, Storage → Warehouse → Silo, Trading Post → Market Hall) grows where it stands. The old building's gold and levels count towards the new one, and the pipes stay.

Levels stop at 25

  • Every level adds 10% output (and input), so level 25 makes 9.85× level 1.
  • A level step costs what that copy cost to build, and 15% more for every level it already has: the step from 24 to 25 costs 25 times the copy's price, and all 24 steps together 184 times. So your 40th Wind Moily's levels cost 14 times your first one's, and growing means building wider, not only higher.
  • From level 11, levels also need goods worth 30% of the step's gold, made in the building's own Era: planks and bricks for the steps to levels 11–15, then also iron ingots and glass (16–20), then also copper ingots (21–25). An Era-2 building needs steel and concrete, then copper wire, then aluminium. Your storages keep what your next level needs; what you don't make comes from your Yard at your neighbours' price or from the market at 2.5×. Every plot lacks one basic, so every plot needs a friend's bricks, glass or copper ingots to grow.
  • A building shows a star at levels 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25, and looks grander at each (bronze, silver, gold, copper trim, and at 25 the owner's pennant with a golden glow).
  • The cap is the point: with a fixed plot and a fixed top level, a plot has a ceiling we can calculate. Research then matters as much as levels, and every big price in the game is set against that ceiling.

Step costs are in multiples of what that copy cost to build; goods are worth 30% of the step's gold on top. Research multiplies on top of the levels (§12).

Sleeping buildings

A building from a later Era than your town's sleeps: it shows a moon, makes and uses nothing, and costs nothing. It wakes when the town reaches its Era. This happens when you move to a town one Era below your own (§11).

  • A building whose pipe is full shows one door on its panel: the next tier on its links, then the levels the new pipe carries, with the gold a minute it would add. Draw a better pipe over an old one and it upgrades where it lies.
  • Power lines (Era 2) carry only energy, lose nothing, have no limit and cross water.
  • Valves let chosen goods pass; priority valves choose which side is served first. A network needs a Pump Station for every 50 buildings.

One pipe, every kind of transport

The pipe is the game's heart, so it should show what it does. In 1.4 the pipe is a big conduit with three lanes inside: power cables, a conveyor belt and a slim fluid line. Where it plugs into a building, the lane that building needs comes out through a brass hatch on the side of the pipe, so you can read a plot's connections at a glance.

What movesGoodsThe connectorHow it moves
Energyenergytwo or three copper cables on tiny postsyellow sparks run along them
Solidsevery ore, coal, stone, sand and wood, and every made good, from ingots and bricks to robots and spaceframes a short conveyor belt on little legsthe goods ride on it, in their colours
Fluidswater, oila slim pipe of its own with a red valve wheela glint of water or oil flows through it

The rules

  • One connector per kind. A building gets a connector for each kind of good it takes or makes: a Wind Moily cables; an Iron Mine cables and a belt; a Water Pump cables and a slim pipe; a Coal Plant all three. A Storage or trading post shows the kinds that are moving through it right now.
  • They move only when goods move. The belt rolls in the direction of the flow, the sparks run towards whoever uses the energy, the fluid glints. A building that stands still has still connectors, so an idle building shows at once.
  • The big pipe keeps its glowing pellets in the goods' colours. The connectors show what kind of transport it is; the pellets show which good.
  • The pipe's tier shows on the hatches and connectors too: iron, copper, blue steel, glass, violet superconductor trim.
  • Look inside: hovering a pipe (or holding Alt) turns it see-through, like the cutaway, showing what runs in each lane and how full it is.
  • Zoomed out, the connectors fade so the map stays calm; close up they're one of the nicest things to watch.
  • Power lines (Era 2) plug into the pipe's cable lane where they meet it.

How it's made: each good gets a kind in the content files (power, solid or fluid). The connectors are rendered pieces, like the pipes themselves (art/pipes.mjs), not generated pictures, so they line up exactly with every pipe shape and building plate: three kinds, four directions, one trim per tier, side by side when a building needs more than one. The goods on the belts are the resource icons. These Codex mock-ups set the look.

Each Era also opens more room: the outskirts in Era 2, the Deep Level in Era 3, the wilderness in Era 4. With levels capped at 25, land is how a plot keeps growing.

How a town moves up

  • Each town has its own Era. It moves up when its Era Wonder is finished (§13), and never by a deadline: an Era is earned. A town where nobody plays stays where it is.
  • The new Era starts for everyone living in the town, also those who are away.
  • Towns race each other on the world map: "Ironvale reached Era 3 first".

When the Era begins

  • The Era's buildings appear in the build menu, its deposits on your land wake up, and its tracks and Era research open.
  • The market buys and sells the new goods, and wants half as much again of the older ones.
  • A launch party in the hub: everyone in the town makes 10% more for a day. Loady opens the Era's chapter: what's new and where to start.
  • Your Yard gets a new Monument site.

Your Era and moving

  • Your Era is the highest Era a town reached while you lived in it. It never goes down.
  • Newcomers start in an Era-1 town. You can move to towns of your own Era or one below, never higher: to reach Era 3 you help a town get there.
  • In a town below your Era, your buildings from the higher Era sleep until the town catches up. Your research stays yours, but its higher-Era tracks only work on awake buildings. Moving down is for playing with newer friends, not for carrying their town.
  • Strong players can't rush a younger town's Wonder either: every stage takes at least a day to build once it's full, so an Era takes at least three days whoever pays for it.

How long an Era takes

An Era ends when the town finishes its Wonder, and Wonders have fixed sizes (rule 2), so a town with more active players gets there sooner. From the model (§17), for regular players who give half of their late-phase gold:

Active players in the town124816
Era 2 begins on day332317129
Era 2 lastsmore than 3 weeksmore than 3 weeksmore than 3 weeks21 days14 days

Eras 3 to 5 are sized the same way in phase C, aiming at three to five weeks each for a town of eight, about four months from an empty plot to a launch.

12 · Research

Research is where you choose what you're good at. It costs gold and goods when it starts, but mostly it costs time, and time can't be bought. The basic tiers take minutes, the big ones days.

Tracks

Deep research for one chain: its mine and its factories. Nine tiers over about ten days. This is what makes a specialist fifteen times better than someone who didn't research.

The Era tree

Short research that opens your Era's pipes, buildings and systems: minutes in Era 1, a day in Era 5.

  • Research needs a Lab (Level 4). Each of the two lines works on one thing at a time, with a queue of five, and keeps going while you're away. Two lines, so a two-day track tier never holds up a pipe you need now.
  • Research is yours. Your crew benefits by buying what your mastered chain makes.

A track, tier by tier

TierTakesDone afterWhat it doesGold (Era-1 track)Goods
110 min10 minFaster ×1.25500—
21 hour1 h 10 minLeaner: 20% less input3,000—
34 hours5 hoursFaster ×1.5 (×1.9 in all)20,000the chain's own good, worth about a fifth of the gold
412 hours17 hoursComplexes100,000

82 days7.2 daysMega complexes20 million

  • Faster: the chain's buildings work faster. Everything they take and make goes up together, like extra levels, so a faster mine digs more from the same deposit.
  • Leaner: the chain's buildings need less of every input, energy included, for the same output. For wind, sun and water power it means 20% and 30% more output instead, for fuel-burning plants less fuel.
  • Complexes: four of the chain's 1×1 buildings in a square merge into one 2×2 building with the output of five; mega complexes: nine in a 3×3 square give the output of twelve. Bigger buildings get +25% and +33% instead.
  • Master: the last ×2, golden trim on the chain's buildings, and a title: "Iron Master".
  • Tracks of later Eras cost four times as much gold per Era. Their times are the same: ten days is ten days.
  • Nothing gets cheaper because others have it. That would push everyone to research the same thing, the opposite of what the game wants. Late towns get help with their Wonders instead (§13).

The gold of each tier is a few hours of a player's income when they typically reach it: tier 5 of a first track on day 2, when 500,000 g is about 20 minutes of income; tier 9 on day 10, when 50 million is about 3 hours. Later tracks come when incomes are higher, so they feel cheaper. Research takes 1–15% of a player's spending (§17).

Deep beats wide, alone or together

The model (§17) played the same plots two ways: the first two tiers of everything and then one track to the top, or every track up a tier at a time. Going deep costs a little at first (wide is 6–8% ahead in the first two weeks) and pays from the third: 17% more gold by day 21 and 39% more by day 30, for every one of the four tracks tried. So the game advises everyone to go deep: the research panel shows what each tier adds in gold a minute, and Loady suggests your richest chain. In a crew, each resident going deep on a different track means the Yard has a master for every chain.

A master's market grows with them: every tier of a track raises your Hub Orders for that track's goods by 30% (×10.6 at tier 9), so a master isn't drowned by their own flood. Without it, a Copper or Sand master earned 40% less than a player who went wide.

The Power track counts half (each of its faster tiers gives half its boost: ×4.75 instead of ×15), because every building uses energy. Even so, a Power master earns a third to a half more than the others by day 30, and Copper is the weakest. Phase B evens them out with the bots: the smaller chains' tracks can also cover the Era-2 buildings that use their goods (Copper the Wire Mill, Stone and Sand the Cement Kiln), and their rich deposits can grow.

13 · Wonders and Monuments

Two kinds of shared project, and after the last Era a third:

The Monument · your Yard

Built with gold by the residents, in stages without end. Every stage makes every resident a little better. Four friends pay for one Monument and all four get it.

The Era Wonder · your town

Built with goods by everyone in the town, in three stages. Each stage gives the town a perk; the last brings the next Era.

Missions · after the Space Elevator

Launches without end, each a little bigger, each a lasting bonus and a star for the town.

Their sizes are fixed numbers, the same in every town and every Yard however many people play (rule 2). More people get them done sooner because more people make more.

The Era Wonder

  • Giving goods. Each good has a "give" switch with two settings: beyond my Hub Order (the spare the market would pay least for) or all spare. Either way it comes after your own buildings, links and Yard (§8). You can also give from your storages or the Yard's Depot at any time.
  • Giving gold. "Buy and give" buys the goods a stage still needs from the market at 2.5× and gives them: a way to turn gold into the next Era when nothing else is worth buying.
  • Giving is a gift: no gold comes back. You get a share of the rewards and the Era itself. The goods leave the game, which makes the Wonder the town's big sink.
  • A stage takes at least a day to build once it's full, so an Era takes at least three days whoever pays for it. Strong players can't rush a younger town.
  • The trail is blazed: each town that finished a Wonder before makes it 10% smaller for the towns after it, down to half. Late towns catch up.
  • Rewards by your share of the stage: Bronze 1%, Silver 3%, Gold 7%, Diamond 15% of what the stage needed. They pay 1, 3, 6 or 12 hours of your own income and a title; Diamond builders get a statue in the hub. Every giver's colour is on the Wonder; nobody is listed for not giving.

The first two are worked out in §17: the Great Dynamo is finished on day 12 by a town of eight regular players who give half of their late-phase gold, on day 9 by sixteen and on day 33 by one. The later ones follow the same rule and are checked in phase C. Every perk is for everyone in the town and lasts for good.

The Launch and missions

  • When a town's Space Elevator is finished, it launches: a countdown, a show in the hub, titles for every giver, statues for the Diamond builders, and Legacy for every player in the town (account perks for any future company: a manager slot, starting gold, cosmetics, never enough to outrun newcomers).
  • Then missions begin: each asks for Era-5 goods, 10% more than the last, starting at a fixed size set with the Space Elevator in phase C. Each one finished gives the town +1% production for good and a star on the world map. They never end, so the town's goods always have somewhere to go.
  • The world map ranks towns by Era, launches and stars.

The Monuments

Each Era gives the Yard one Monument site, in the Yard's square. The crew picks which of the five to build there, so by Era 5 a Yard has five, in its own order. A Monument is built with gold, by any resident, in stages without end: the first stage of an Era-1 Monument costs 100 million gold and each stage 40% more than the last.   • The Grand Fountain, Clock Tower, Observatory and Lighthouse have art already (today they are district Wonders); the Workshop needs a picture. Each one grows grander every five stages.

"Typical day" is when the regular player of §17 got there. Buildings of Eras 2–5 come with the town's Era, not with a level. After Level 25 each level needs 1.47 times the gold of the one before.

The journey

Era 1 · Steam & Iron · about 12 days in a town of eight

  • The first evening: from an empty plot to Level 6, 170 buildings and the first chains (§17).
  • Days 1–5, building up: levels, a parcel every day or two, copper pipes, the first research tiers, complexes on your track. You pin "I make energy" on the Plan board.
  • Days 5–12, the late phase: the plot is built; the Monument's stages, the Great Dynamo's stages and your track's big tiers.
  • Day 12: the Dynamo's last stage. Era 2.

Decisions: which track, which parcel, which Monument, who in the Yard makes what, how much to give.

Era 2 · Electric · about three weeks

  • Steel needs ingots and coal, wire needs copper ingots: the Yard re-wires itself around the new chains.
  • Bauxite wakes on three of the four plots. Aluminium eats energy: the power specialist's big moment.
  • The outskirts: nine more parcels each, holding every resource, all bought in about nine days.
  • Income triples within a few days, then the late phase again: a second Monument, the Copper Cathedral.

Era 3 · Oil & Machines · 3–4 weeks

  • Oil wakes in the deserts; refineries make plastic; gears and motors need three chains each.
  • The Deep Level under your plot: dig out parcels over days for rich ore, magma power and a huge Vault.
  • Trunk lines: your Yard's links reach other towns.
  • The Terraformer: raise a hill, drain a lake, or seed the deposit your plot lacks.
  • The Grand Refinery Tower.

Era 4 · Electronics · 4–5 weeks

  • Rare earth; circuits, batteries and robots. A robot needs every land resource.
  • The wilderness opens: up to three outposts on rich deposits, Discoveries every four days, Quantum Links to bring it home.
  • The Thinking Machine.

Era 5 · Space Age · 5–6 weeks

  • Titanium from the mountains, superconductors, spaceframes; the Fusion Reactor.
  • Superconductor pipes: no limits, no losses.
  • The Space Elevator: the town's biggest project, then the Launch.

After the Launch

  • Missions without end, each a lasting bonus and a star.
  • Mastering the tracks you skipped; a perfect plot; decorations; the rankings.
  • Moving down an Era to play with newer friends (your higher buildings sleep).

Something to do at every pace

RhythmWhat
SecondsCoins popping, goods flowing, a building finishing
MinutesBuilding, levels, the next Company Level, early research tiers
HoursStorages filling, daily orders, the Era tree, mid tiers, Monument stages
DaysThe big tiers, parcels, Wonder stages, events, digging the Deep Level
WeeksEras, mastering tracks, the outskirts, the Launch

15 · Alone and together

Playing alone

  • The market buys everything you make and sells everything you lack. Your plot has six of the eight land resources, plus water, iron ore and wood, so it can do all of Era 1 by itself.
  • A missing resource costs you, but doesn't block you. A Smelter on coal bought from the market at 2.5× still adds 10 g per tile instead of 25. From Era 2 your outskirts hold every resource.
  • You research like everyone: the first tiers of every track, then one track to the top (§12).
  • Nothing is made smaller because you're alone (rule 2). Your Monument costs what it costs a crew, and your town's Wonder what it costs a full town. A lone player in an empty town reaches Era 2 around day 33; in a town with others much sooner, and anyone can move to a livelier town of their Era.
  • You can trade with anyone: links to other Yards, the Exchange to every town.

Playing together: what a crew gets

Ana, Ben, Cleo and Dev share a Yard. Each lacks a different basic; on day one they pin their plans on the Plan board: Ana goes deep in Power, Ben in Iron, Cleo in Sand and Dev in Copper. The model played them against the same four players each alone in a Yard, with the same plots, research and visits (§17).

What we aim for

A crew member earns 5–10% more than a solo player in the first week and 10–20% more after. Living in a busy town matters more: its Wonder brings the next Era a week or two sooner, and an Era triples income. That's worth finding friends for, and never a reason to quit when you play alone. The bots in phase B measure it on the real server (§23).

The first version of this plan aimed for twice the income by day 28. The model showed that this needs plots that can't work alone, which would break rule 1, so the aim is lower and honest.

16 · Gold and goods: where they go

The last AI playtest showed players spending 0.2% of their gold: it piled up with nowhere to go. In this design gold always has a next step, and the model in §17 checks it: from day 5 a regular player spends more than 90% of everything they earn and never holds more than about four hours of income.

Gold comes from

  • The market, up to your Hub Orders and less beyond them
  • Other players paying your prices
  • Daily orders, Wonder rewards, expeditions, achievements

Goods go to

  • Your own and your friends' buildings
  • Your and your friends' levels from level 11 (§9)
  • The market
  • The Wonder and missions (gone for good)
  • Research tiers and the costs of Era 2–5 buildings (gone for good)

Where gold goes

The ceiling, and what comes after it

A building tops out at 9.85× from levels and 15× from a mastered track; a plot at 16 parcels and, from Era 2, nine outskirts. So a plot has a ceiling in each Era, and an engaged player reaches most of it in about five days. After that, every level and copy left takes more than a week to pay for itself. The Era's late phase answers it: the Monument turns gold into a little more for every resident, the Wonder turns it into the next Era, and the next Era brings new buildings, goods, land and tracks, so paybacks fall back to hours. Big prices are set from the model's incomes, never from how many people play.

17 · A base, day by day: the numbers worked out

Every number in this document was checked by playing it. A model plays a plot minute by minute with exactly the rules of §8 to §16 and the formulas of §22: the land and its deposits, wind and sun, Hub Orders, copies and levels and their goods, research, Company Level, parcels, the outskirts, the Monument and the Wonder. This section shows what came out: what a base looks like, what it earns, and where its gold goes. The model's code is in docs/design-notes/v1.4/sim, with how to run it.

The player in the model
  • Visits three times a day: ten minutes at 8:00, forty-five at 19:30, ten at 22:30. The first evening is two hours.
  • Does about two things a minute: place a building, Max one building, start research or buy a parcel.
  • Always buys what pays for itself soonest, keeps research running, buys land when it's useful, and ignores anything that takes longer than five days to pay back.
  • When nothing pays back within five days, puts its gold into the Yard's Monument and the town's Wonder, half each, and keeps two hours of income.
  • Lacks sand (and oil), has its rich deposit in iron, and researches the first two tiers of every track, then Iron to the top, then Steel once Era 2 opens.

It is a tireless and sensible player, not a person: it never forgets, never plays for fun, never decorates. People will be slower and less exact. Its numbers are the ceiling of normal play, which is what the prices have to be set against. The bots in phase B play the same rules on the real server and must agree (§23).

Keen: four visits a day153,383269,5441,164,8732,161,89520 · 25 · 30

A once-a-day player who uses the game's one-tap helpers (Max on a building, Grow on the plot: spend on whatever pays back soonest) keeps up with a regular one, because what holds a plot back after the first days is the next parcel, the next research tier and the next Era, not the clicks. Without the helpers, the same player is three or four days behind and banks a day of income at each visit. The helpers are part of phase A.

The rhythm of an Era

  1. Building up (days 0–3). Everything pays back in minutes, then hours. Gold goes to buildings, levels, research and parcels. Income grows twentyfold from day 1 to day 3.
  2. Filling the plot (days 3–5). The start area and the first parcels are built and mostly at level 15 to 25. The next level of anything takes days to pay back; the next parcel waits for the next Company Level.
  3. The Era's late phase (day 5 to the Wonder). Gold that would only buy week-long paybacks goes to the Yard's Monument (every stage makes every resident 3% more productive) and the town's Wonder (the next Era). New parcels and research tiers keep coming and are bought at once. Gold never piles up: from day 5 the player spends over 90% of what they earn and holds one to four hours of income.
  4. The next Era (day 12 in a town of eight). New buildings, new goods with fresh Hub Orders, the outskirts and new tracks: paybacks drop to hours again, and income triples within a few days. Then the same rhythm.
Why gold no longer piles up

In the AI playtests players spent 0.2% of their gold. The model shows why any version of this game would end that way: a plot is a fixed size, levels stop at 25 and the market pays less for floods, so after a few days nothing a player can buy pays back within a week, however the prices are set. Making things dearer only moves the moment. The answer is the late phase: a Monument that never runs out of stages and a Wonder that leads somewhere, both sized in gold the plot really makes, and the next Era as the reward.

18 · Away, moving and leaving

Away

  • Everything keeps running: buildings, trade, research and gifts with "give" on. Coming back shows the offline report: what you earned, what filled up, what finished.
  • Nothing is lost by not playing, and nothing changes for your neighbours: your plot keeps making and buying what it did. A link's two-hour tank and the Yard's fallback cover any gap.
  • Your plot stays yours, however long you're gone. Towns open new land for newcomers instead.

Moving

  • Free, five minutes between moves, to any free plot in a town of your Era or one below (into a closed Yard with a resident's yes).
  • Your plot is packed and unpacked in the new place: the layout stays where the land allows, and buildings that don't fit (a mine with no deposit there) become crates with their levels, placed later or scrapped for 75%. Workshops come along as crates.
  • Your outskirts parcels are bought back for half their price, their buildings into crates. Your gold, research, levels, Era and titles come with you.
  • The plot you left is empty land again.

Leaving a Yard

  • Moving away ends your crew membership. The last resident to leave is warned that the Yard's Monuments, Depot and decorations will be torn down, and confirms.
  • A Yard whose residents all stopped playing stays as it is, closed or open. Pick for me never sends anyone to a Yard where nobody plays.

19 · Everything else in the game

Loady and the Next steps card

Loady guides the first hour and opens a chapter at each Era: what's new and where to start. The Next steps card always shows the three best things to do, worked out from your real networks.

Daily orders

Three orders a day from the market, for goods you make, paying twice the base price for what fills them.

Events

Storms (wind ×2, some damage), heatwaves (sun ×1.5), droughts, cold snaps (the market wants energy), expos (a good sells for three times as much for six hours), shortages, and from Era 4 Discoveries in the wilderness. Announced a day ahead, three with a Weather Station.

Managers

Jo repairs storm damage, Bea sells what overflows, Rick upgrades what pays back within two hours, Lin renews good links, Sam keeps your research queues full. Slots at Levels 10, 20, 30 and 45, plus one from Automation (Era 4). Max and Grow do the same in one tap for everyone (§17).

The Deep Level (Era 3)

A second 32×32 layer under your plot. Parcels are dug out, hours for the first and days for the last, giving stone and ore while they dig. Rich ★3–★5 ore, magma for energy, a Vault, pipes that lose nothing. Mines, power and storage only: factories stay above ground. Deep Lifts carry goods up.

The wilderness (Era 4)

Up to three outposts of 8×8 on rich deposits between the towns, leased by the week. Discoveries add new ones every four days. Goods come home by Cargo Depot or Quantum Link.

Expeditions (Level 20)

Send a team out for 1, 4 or 12 hours: gold, decorations, relics with a story, blueprints; from Era 4 also where the next rich deposit lies.

Showing off

Decorations, golden collection pieces, buildings that grow grander at every five levels, photo mode, visiting and likes, and the rankings of Yards and towns.

Talking

Yard chat, town chat, world chat and direct messages, with blocking and reporting.

Blueprints and achievements

Save a layout and rebuild it in one go. Achievements and collections give gold, titles and golden decorations.

20 · The wilderness and other towns: still open

The one part that isn't designed yet

How the wilderness is used and how towns deal with each other is left open on purpose. 1.4 only prepares for it, so whatever we pick later fits without moving anyone. Below: what 1.4 already has, what it prepares, and ideas to choose from. None of the ideas is a decision.

Already in 1.4

  • The Exchange trades with every town from Level 12, by cargo that takes time.
  • Trunk lines (Era 3): a Yard lays its own pipe through the wilderness to another town's gate, for its members' links.
  • Outposts and Discoveries (Era 4): up to three claims of 8×8 on rich deposits, by the week.
  • Expeditions and the race between towns on the world map.

What 1.4 prepares

  • 128 tiles of wilderness between towns (today 30): four plots wide, room for long lines, claims and whatever comes next.
  • Four town gates per town, where its two roads leave it: where lines from other towns arrive.
  • Wilderness with a shape: rivers, mountains, forests and rich deposits, so a route between towns is a puzzle.
  • Distance matters: over 128 tiles a grey pipe delivers 68%, copper 82%, steel 94%, composite 97%, glass 99%, and only superconductor 100%.

Your idea, worked out a little: the pipe master and carrier lines

  • A Pipes track. A 22nd research track, for transport instead of a good: pipes that cost less per tile, lose less and carry more, pump houses further apart. Its master tier unlocks superconductor lines through the wilderness: lossless, and buildable before Era 5, or only by Pipe Masters at all. Pipe Master becomes a role in a Yard, like the power specialist.
  • Rights of way. The carrier rents a strip of wilderness from one town gate to another, by the week. Lines may cross each other with a bridge but never share a tile, and whoever claims a good route first has it.
  • The line is the gate between two towns. Players in either town plug in at their own town gate and send goods across. Under the hood it's a highway for links: each trade on it is still between two named players (or a player and the other town's market), and the line adds its loss and the carrier's fee.
  • The carrier runs it as a business: sets the fee (say up to 10% of the goods' base value), decides who comes first when it's full (usual users first, as in the Yard), and upgrades its tier and width. Lines show on the world map in the carrier's colours.
  • Why people would pay: the other town's players to trade with, the other town's market (a second set of Hub Orders at the full price), and goods their own town hardly makes.
  • Young towns feed old ones. Goods only flow to towns of their Era or later, and an Era-4 town's chains eat huge amounts of ingots and bricks. A new town has buyers from day one, and the carrier has a business.

More ideas for the wilderness

Seams that run out

Rich ★5 deposits that last a few weeks and then run dry, while Discoveries add new ones elsewhere. The wilderness map keeps changing, and so do the best routes.

Caravan camps

Neutral markets between two towns where anyone from either town trades at player prices. No town market there: only people.

Twin towns

Two towns joined by a line become twins: each one's goods count for the other's Wonder, and goods from the twin get bigger Hub Orders.

Joint projects

A bridge, a dam or a railway between towns, built by both together, with a perk for every town it joins: the first Wonder for more than one town.

Fog and expeditions

The wilderness starts unexplored. Expeditions map it and find deposits, good routes and ruins with relics.

Lodges in the wild

Later, a small plot of your own out in the wilderness: a base for a carrier or a miner who wants to live between towns.

What we'd have to decide

  1. Who may build lines between towns: anyone, a Yard together, or only Pipe Masters?
  2. When it opens: with trunk lines in Era 3, or earlier.
  3. How a full line is shared, and whether the carrier's fee is free or capped.
  4. What happens to a line when its carrier stops playing: it keeps running (as everything else does), but who pays the rent?
  5. Whether players may sell to another town's market over a line, or only trade with its players.
  6. Whether towns stay fully separate in their Eras (my advice: yes, lines carry goods, never Eras).

Stays: pipes and the flow solver, the Hub Orders (fixed now), the HQ and trading post, Loady and the Next steps card, the art of almost every building, the Wonders' art, evolve in place, complexes (now from tracks), the Exchange, links, the Deep Level, outposts, expeditions, terraforming, blueprints, events, managers, achievements, photo mode, moving with crates.

22 · The numbers

23 · Building it

Four phases. Each lands on the test server when it's done and stays playable. The test world is wiped at the start of phase A, and again at B or C if the content needs it.

PhaseWhat you getHow it's checked
A · Your own place
about a week		 The new map (towns, side Yards, start areas against the Yard, outskirts land set aside, the six-of-eight land, 128 tiles of wilderness between towns with a town gate where each road leaves the town); starting from scratch; picking your spot on the map, links, Pick for me, requests; Yard = crew with owners, open or closed, the last-one-out rule; no Houses or stand-ins; your own prices and the stalls; nothing that depends on how many people play (quiet grace and every size from active players go); Max and Grow, the one-tap helpers that keep spending up with income; the bots learn to play like the model of §17 Game tests; e2e with four browsers finding each other on the map and a phone; the bots' first hour from nothing; big-estate on the new layout
B · The economy
1–2 weeks		 Levels capped at 25, priced per copy, with goods from level 11; the market of §8 (fixed Hub Orders, the trading post's reach, masters' Hub Orders, no unit limit); Company Level from gold earned; the new Era-1 and Era-2 recipes and prices; the two research lines with every Era-1 and Era-2 track, Power at half; per-town Eras with the Great Dynamo and the Copper Cathedral at their fixed sizes, gifts, "buy and give" and rewards; the endless Monuments; the Era rules for moving and sleeping buildings; the outskirts; art for the Bauxite Pit and the Aluminium Works The bots play the real server like the model of §17 for 35 days, alone and in crews: they must land on the model's numbers in §22 within a fifth, and the tracks must stay within a third of each other
C · Eras 3 to 5
1–2 weeks plus art		 Oil, rare earth and titanium; the new goods and buildings with their art (Motor Works, Battery Works, Titanium Mine, Titanium Works, Spaceframe Works, the Workshop Monument, the stalls, the composite pipe); the pipe's three lanes and their connectors; the Deep Level and the wilderness in their Eras; trunk lines; the Space Elevator, the Launch, missions and Legacy The art steps in CLAUDE.md for every new building; screenshots of each Era
D · Balance and polish
about a week		 The bots play a whole town for 120 days; Hub Orders, costs and Wonder sizes tuned; GameDesign.md rewritten from this plan; e2e scripts updated, the retired ones removed Pacing targets (§22); every e2e script

New art is made with Codex on your personal account or Ketty's, never the Xebia one.

24 · What could go wrong

Friends trade less than you'd hopeEvery plot can do Era 1 by itself (rule 1), so in the model trade between friends is 2–15% of a crew's income, about what the playtests saw. 1.4 doesn't pretend otherwise: a crew's edge comes as much from the shared Monument as from trading, and the goods for levels give friends something real to sell each other from the second week. If people want more trade, the levers are the share of goods in levels (30% now) and how many resources a plot lacks.
  • The Era's late phase feels flat. After about five days the plot is built and its income grows slowly until the Wonder. Research tiers, Monument stages, the Wonder's stages and new parcels keep something happening at every visit, and §17 shows gold never piles up; whether it's fun is for people to tell us.
  • The model is a bot. It plays tirelessly and well. People will be slower, so the real pace is a little behind §17, never ahead. The helpers (Max, Grow) close most of the gap, and phase B's bots check the real server against the model.
  • Tracks aren't equal. Even at half strength, a Power master earns a third to a half more than the others by day 30, and Copper is the weakest. Phase B tunes them with the bots.
  • Ten-day tracks feel slow. Tiers 1–4 finish on day one, the Era tree runs beside them, and the research panel shows what each tier will add in gold a minute, so a two-day tier is something to look forward to.
  • A lone player in a quiet town waits long for Era 2. About day 33 by themselves, against day 12 in a town of eight. That's rule 2 at work. Pick for me never sends newcomers to an empty town, and anyone can move to a livelier town of their Era for free.
  • A late friend lands in a different town. They can trade over the Exchange from day one, the trail makes their Wonders smaller, and the older friend can move down one Era to join them.
  • Numbers get huge. A plot earns millions a minute in Era 2 and Wonders cost billions. The interface already shortens numbers (12.4M), and idle players like seeing them grow.
  • A lot of today's code goes. Houses, stand-ins, seats, kits, corporations, contracts, quiet grace and more. The solver, the pipes and the art stay, and every phase is playable on its own.
  • Bigger worlds per player. Plots stay 32×32, but with the outskirts and the Deep Level a late plot is about 2.5 times as many tiles, and the model's plot has 800 buildings on day 34. The big-estate check measures it in phases A and C.

25 · My picks you may want to change

You asked me to fill in the gaps and then to work the numbers out. These are the choices I made, newest first, so they're the ones worth a look:

  1. Goods for levels: from level 11 a level step also needs goods worth 30% of its gold. It gives friends something to sell each other and Era-1 goods a use beyond the market.
  2. The Monument: paid in gold, with stages that never end, 40% dearer each; one site per Era. It's where the late-phase gold goes, and four friends pay for one.
  3. The Wonder: fixed sizes in goods (the Great Dynamo 4.8 billion gold's worth), "buy and give" with gold at the market's 2.5×, each stage at least a day. No "half the town" rule.
  4. The market: 1,000 g a minute of every Era-1 good, the trading post's level as the way to grow it, and research raising it for your own goods (×1.3 a tier), so a master isn't drowned by their own flood.
  5. Company Level from gold earned alone, and parcels at every second level from 5 to 27.
  6. The Power track at half strength, because every building uses energy, and masters' Hub Orders 30% bigger a tier, so going deep pays for every track.
  7. Crew target lowered to +5–10% in week 1 and 10–20% after, from the model.
  8. Land: every plot has water, iron ore and wood; each lacks one of copper ore, coal, stone and sand, and one of bauxite, oil, rare earth and titanium ore.
  9. Research: two lines, the deep tracks and a short Era tree. Tracks are nine tiers over about ten days. Nothing gets cheaper because others researched it.
  10. The outskirts: nine parcels set aside for each plot from Era 2, rather than first-come land between the Yards.
  11. New Yards are open unless the first resident closes it. Workshops: each resident may build on up to 64 tiles of the Yard's ends.
  12. The end: each town launches its own Space Elevator and then does missions; there's no world-wide season ending.
  13. What goes: corporations (crews and towns instead), contracts (links instead), the Franchise and branch estates (moving and the outskirts instead), and the Bank, Showroom and Pneumatic Post.

The wilderness and how towns deal with each other (§20) is the one part left open on purpose; 1.4 only makes room for it.

If this is the game you want, I'll start with phase A.
